pedagogy.summary: At 7-8, children learn (still with teacher support) to break a multi-step problem into sub-problems, choose and sequence strategies, and check answers for reasonableness using estimation and inverse operations. This is where the keyword strategy becomes actively harmful: research on released test items shows that tying a word to an operation succeeds on fewer than half of single-step problems and under 10% of multi-step problems, so a habit that seemed to 'work' earlier now fails badly. The parallel risk is the compulsion to calculate — producing an answer with no estimate benchmark and no check. Effective teaching builds the estimate-first-then-verify routine, teaches self-monitoring via modelled self-questioning (strong evidence), and uses visual representations to expose the sequence of steps (strong evidence), while normalising strategy-switching when the first approach stalls.
bestPractices: Estimate first to set a reasonableness benchmark, then compute, then check by an inverse operation or a different method — revise if they disagree
Teach problem structure (schema), not keywords: the keyword strategy collapses on multi-step problems (match rate <10%)
Model self-questioning aloud and provide a prompt list for monitoring progress across the sub-steps (WWC Rec 2, strong evidence)
Represent the problem with a bar/strip diagram so the sub-problems and their order are visible (WWC Rec 3, strong evidence)
Break the problem into named sub-problems and solve each, keeping the whole plan in view
Normalise strategy-switching: if the first approach stalls, deliberately try a different representation or method rather than abandoning
keyRepresentations: Bar / strip diagram decomposing a multi-step problem into sub-parts
Number line for sequencing multi-step jumps
Estimation / rounding to a benchmark before computing
Inverse-operation check (work backwards to the start)
A monitoring prompt list across the sub-steps: plan → do a step → check → next
commonMisconceptions: Keyword strategy on multi-step problems — tying a word to an operation and applying operations in the wrong order
Computing an answer with no estimate and no check, accepting answers that are wildly off (compulsion to calculate)
Believing that if the first method doesn't work, you're simply stuck (no strategy-switching)
Doing the sub-steps but not connecting them — losing track of what has been found and what remains

learn.summary: For ages 7-8 (with teacher support): make sense of multi-step problems within 1000 by breaking them into ordered sub-problems, choosing and sequencing strategies, estimating a reasonableness benchmark first, and checking with an inverse operation or a different method — revising when the two disagree. The central aim is to replace the keyword habit (tying a word to an operation), which research on released items reports succeeds on under 50% of single-step and under 10% of multi-step problems, with attention to problem structure, and to counter the compulsion to calculate (answering with no estimate and no check). Self-questioning aloud and visual representations (e.g. bar/strip diagrams and number lines for sequencing jumps) are the two levers cited with strong evidence in the WWC grades 4-8 guide; strategy-switching when the first approach stalls should be normalised.

activities.title: Estimate-first multi-step solver with inverse check
feedback: If a child seizes on 'left' and subtracts 50 from 320 immediately, never forming the 4×50 sub-step: have them retell and represent the problem as ordered sub-problems on a strip diagram, and discuss why the cue word misleads here

When a keyword-driven wrong-order calculation lands far from the estimate and working backwards through the story (adding back all 200 pencils sold, e.g. 270 + 200 = 470, not 320) fails to return the starting number, point out the two mismatches and invite re-sequencing the steps
If the answer is 'more left than it started with' and the child is untroubled: require an estimate before computing and an inverse/alternative check after — do not reteach the arithmetic itself

If the child stalls and stops, model 'change course if necessary': show a second way to represent the same problem — for instance switching from a strip/bar diagram to a number line of the multi-step jumps — and name switching as a normal part of solving
activities.rationale: Operationalises the two strong-evidence WWC levers (visual representation of the problem structure and monitoring) and the plan-monitor-check-revise practice described in SMP1, while directly targeting the keyword habit the keyword-investigation reports as failing on multi-step problems. Optional interactive affordances (sequenceable sub-problem cards on a bar-model canvas, an estimate slider, an inverse-check panel that works backwards, a reasonableness gauge, and a 'try another way' button) are illustrations of how to make these signals visible, not required mechanisms; the same can be done on paper with a drawn strip diagram or number line and a written-out backwards check.
sourceClaims: Tying a keyword to an operation leads to a correct solution less than 50% of the time on single-step routine problems and under 10% on multi-step problems (0% for the comparison schema) — keywords are an ineffective strategy educators should avoid in favour of schema instruction.

Modelling a self-questioning process to help students monitor and reflect (Rec 2) and teaching students to build and use visual representations of the problem (Rec 3) each have strong evidence for improving problem solving in grades 4-8.
Proficient solvers plan a solution pathway, monitor and evaluate progress and change course if necessary, and check answers using a different method while asking 'Does this make sense?'.
learnerActions: Take a two-step problem, e.g. 'A shop had 320 pencils. It sold 4 boxes of 50. How many pencils are left?' and arrange it as two connected sub-problem cards in the order you will solve them (first 4×50 = 200 sold, then 320 − 200), adding more cards only if a longer problem needs them
Before computing, state 'about how big' the answer should be — set an estimate benchmark (e.g. 'about 300 sold... no, 200, so a bit over 100 left')
Solve each sub-step in order, keeping the whole plan visible

After you have an answer, work backwards through the story (inverse) to see whether you return to the starting number: put back the pencils that were sold, 120 + 4×50 = 120 + 200 = 320. Undo the actions in the problem, not just your own calculation, because undoing a wrong calculation (e.g. 320 − 50 = 270, then 270 + 50 = 320) would still get you back to 320
Compare your answer against your own estimate: if it is wildly off, treat that as a signal to recheck both the answer and the estimate
If an approach stalls, deliberately re-represent the problem a different way — for example switch between a strip/bar diagram and a number line that sequences the jumps — rather than stopping
activities.intendedInsight: Decomposition is something you physically arrange and sequence, not a rule triggered by a cue word; the estimate and a backwards check that undoes the problem's actions (not merely the child's own calculation) are two separate signals that can catch a wrong-order or wrong-operation answer.

activities.title: Think-aloud study partner for self-monitoring
feedback: Prompt for a plan and an estimate first; withhold steps
When the child states a result, ask 'how could you be sure?' and prompt an inverse or alternative check
If the child treats a stall as failure, ask 'what's another way we could show this?' — for instance a number line instead of a strip diagram — to model switching representations
activities.rationale: Rehearses the modelled self-questioning routine cited with strong evidence, and pressing for justification of sequence and check surfaces decomposition versus keyword-triggered ordering. Spoken, responsive dialogue is well suited to rehearsing self-monitoring aloud, and does not substitute for the child actually doing the arithmetic.
sourceClaims: Modelling a self-questioning process to help students monitor and reflect (Rec 2) and teaching students to build and use visual representations of the problem (Rec 3) each have strong evidence for improving problem solving in grades 4-8.
Proficient solvers plan a solution pathway, monitor and evaluate progress and change course if necessary, and check answers using a different method while asking 'Does this make sense?'.
learnerActions: Work with a partner (or in-role coach) who never hands over the steps but asks you to state a plan and an estimate before computing
Use a monitoring prompt list to pace yourself through the sub-steps: plan → do a step → check → next
Answer monitoring questions aloud: 'What have you found so far? What's still unknown? How could you check that?'
Justify the order you chose for the sub-steps and explain your reasonableness check in your own words
When you are stuck, respond to the prompt to represent the problem a different way — for example a number line for the sequence of jumps — instead of being given the answer
activities.intendedInsight: Self-questioning across sub-steps is a repeatable routine for monitoring progress and catching errors, and being able to explain the sequence and the check shows understanding of the structure.

activities.title: Worked-example reference with revealed self-questions
feedback: Point to the self-question tied to each sub-step so the child connects each move to a reason
Follow up by having the child perform the sequencing and check unaided on a new problem
activities.rationale: A revealed worked example can display the decomposition and the check and acts as a scaffold or reference. On its own it does not have the child sequence the steps or perform the reasonableness check, so it must be paired with independent practice; this is a limitation of the format for this objective, not evidence that a fixed example cannot teach.
sourceClaims: Modelling a self-questioning process to help students monitor and reflect (Rec 2) and teaching students to build and use visual representations of the problem (Rec 3) each have strong evidence for improving problem solving in grades 4-8.
learnerActions: Study a worked multi-step problem where each sub-step can be revealed one at a time
For each revealed sub-step, read the self-question the solver asked and see why the estimate rules certain answers out
After studying, re-solve a fresh but similar problem yourself, sequencing the steps and doing your own check
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the decomposition and the reasonableness reasoning laid out gives a model of what good monitoring looks like before you do it independently.

activities.title: Reasonableness and wrong-order spotting items
feedback: If a child picks an impossible answer, ask them to estimate first and compare against each option
For the runner item, if the child just multiplies, discuss what the situation implies about the real answer (more than 10× the 100 m time, not exactly it)
activities.rationale: Targeted estimation/reasonableness items can probe whether a child reasons about reasonableness and can detect wrong-order calculations. A scored linear format tends to reward fast computing and does not elicit the child's own decomposition or self-monitoring, so it should supplement, not replace, construction tasks.
sourceClaims: The compulsion to calculate leads students to compute without reasoning about reasonableness; realistic/'problematic' items (e.g. the runner and plank problems) show the vast majority of students compute regardless of whether the answer makes sense.
learnerActions: Given a problem and several candidate answers, decide 'which of these answers is impossible, and why?' using estimation
Examine two worked solutions and 'spot the wrong-order calculation' — identify where operations were applied in the wrong sequence

Reason about a realistic item: 'A runner's best time for 100 m is 20 seconds. How long for 1 km?' — explain why it will be more than 10× the 100 m time (tiring over the longer distance), rather than multiplying blindly
activities.intendedInsight: Estimation and attention to the real situation let you reject answers that cannot make sense, even before checking the full computation.

constraints: Teach problem structure (schema), not keywords: cue words like 'left' can trigger the wrong operation or wrong order on multi-step problems.
Always require an estimate benchmark before computing and a check (an inverse that undoes the problem's actions, or a different method) after — revise if they disagree.
Normalise strategy-switching: a stalled first approach is a cue to re-represent the problem (e.g. swap a strip diagram for a number line), not evidence of failure.
Worked, reveal-only examples are scaffolds or references: they show the decomposition and check but do not have the child sequence steps or perform the check — pair them with independent practice.
Scored linear items can assess estimation and wrong-order spotting but do not elicit independent decomposition or self-monitoring and tend to reward fast computing; do not use as the primary task.

Interactive affordances (sequenceable cards, estimate slider, backward-working inverse panel, reasonableness gauge, 'try another way' button) are optional illustrations; the learning can be done on paper with drawn diagrams and written checks.

This multi-step arithmetic content is not spatial, so a 3-D environment adds set-up cost without a clear benefit here — a judgement for this specific content, not a general claim that 3-D media add nothing elsewhere.
At this age children develop the habit with teacher support; independent strategy evaluation comes later, so expect to scaffold the plan-estimate-check routine.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Worked the diagnostic arithmetic independently: 4×50 = 200 sold; 320 − 200 = 120 left; inverse check 120 + 200 = 320. These are consistent across the source and retained as the target reasoning.

The original 'ideal/strong/possible/poor' artefact rankings and the claim that a 3-D environment 'adds cost without benefit' were catalog fit judgements; the non-spatial observation is retained as a content-specific constraint rather than asserted as a universal pedagogical law.

The under-10% multi-step (and under-50% single-step) keyword success figures and the strong-evidence WWC claims are carried from legacy sources marked verified; no independent re-verification was performed in this rewrite.
The legacy 'actively harmful' framing of the keyword strategy is presented here as a low-yield risk, since the cited sources establish low match rates rather than demonstrated harm.

probeDeeper: 'How did you break this into parts — which part did you do first, and why that order?' (surfaces decomposition vs keyword-triggered ordering)
'About how big should the answer be? What tells you a wrong answer is wrong?' (estimate as benchmark)
'Check it a different way — can you work backwards to the 320?' (inverse verification)

Counterexample: 'A runner's best time for 100 m is 20 seconds. How long for 1 km?' — does the child reason about the real situation (it will be more than 10× because of tiring), or just multiply blindly?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who decomposes it (first 4×50 = 200 sold, then 320 − 200), estimates ('about 300 sold... no, 200, so a bit over 100 left'), gets 120, and checks by a different method or inverse (120 + 200 = 320). The decomposition, the estimate benchmark, and a genuine check are the targets.

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword strategy on a multi-step problem — tying a word to an operation and applying operations in the wrong order or using an irrelevant one.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Teach structure over words: have the child retell and represent the problem as ordered sub-problems on a strip diagram; discuss why the cue word misleads here.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child seizes on a word ('left' → subtract) and subtracts 50 from 320 immediately, never forming the 4×50 sub-step; keyword-operation matching is known to succeed under 10% of the time on multi-step problems.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compulsion to calculate: produces an answer with no estimate and no check, accepting results that are clearly unreasonable.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the routine the child already half-knows: require an estimate benchmark before computing and an inverse/alternative check after; do not reteach the arithmetic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives an answer (e.g. 'more left than it started with') and is untroubled; offers no estimate and does not check by inverse when asked what they could do to be sure.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes that if the first method doesn't work, you're stuck — does not switch strategy or representation.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model 'change course if necessary' — show two ways to represent the same problem and name switching as a normal part of solving; prompt 'what's another way we could show this?'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When the first approach stalls the child stops rather than trying a different representation; treats a stall as failure, not as a cue to change course.

responseLevels.gap: Picks an operation from a word, runs steps in the wrong order or uses the wrong numbers, offers no estimate, and accepts an unreasonable answer.
responseLevels.full: Breaks the problem into ordered sub-problems, sets an estimate benchmark, solves, and verifies with an inverse or alternative method — revising when they disagree — switches representation when stuck, and transfers the estimate-then-check routine to a new multi-step problem unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Can decompose the problem and, when prompted, estimate or check — but performs the sub-steps as a disconnected sequence: does not spontaneously use the estimate or an inverse check to catch an error, and stalls rather than switching strategy.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a two-step problem within 1000, e.g. 'A shop had 320 pencils. It sold 4 boxes of 50. How many pencils are left?' Before any answer ask: 'How would you break this into parts? About how big should the answer be? Once you have it, how could you check it a different way?' Then discuss what they did — you are surfacing how they plan, estimate and check, not marking the number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child breaking the problem down reasons about the sub-structure and can state roughly how big the answer must be, then verifies. A child on the keyword habit ties a word to an operation and often runs the steps in the wrong order (e.g. 320 − 50, then ×4) with no estimate to catch it; a compulsion-to-calculate child computes something and accepts it however unreasonable. The estimate and the independent check are where correct and incorrect reasoning diverge — hard to fake either.
